claims.text: The initial Mg-containing alloy is in a non-equilibrium, metastable supersaturated solid-solution state.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous distribution of alloying elements, including Mg.
The as-cast baseline has a uniform phase distribution and stable protective properties.
Exposure at 800–1000 °C can transform a non-equilibrium supersaturated solid solution into equilibrium phases containing an ordered intermetallic phase.
High-temperature oxidative and corrosive service conditions trigger diffusion-controlled nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Thermally activated Mg diffusion is the rate-controlling process for intermetallic nucleation and growth.
Annealing progressively increases the volume fraction of Mg-containing intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitation disrupts the initially uniform matrix.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates impair the stability and integrity of protective surface films.
Intermetallic-induced microstructural heterogeneities act as initiation sites for accelerated corrosion.
Intermetallic-induced microstructural heterogeneities cause breakdown of high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The transformation becomes significant above approximately 800 °C.
A critical dwell time exists beyond which protective properties deteriorate abruptly.
A higher Mg-containing intermetallic volume fraction will correlate with reduced corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
A higher Mg-containing intermetallic volume fraction will correlate with reduced high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
A 3.5 wt% NaCl solution is a controlled environment suitable for evaluating alloy corrosion behavior.
Combined exposure to temperatures at or above 800 °C and 3.5 wt% NaCl represents a realistic combined high-temperature oxidation and corrosion service regime.
